title: The handbook for the road
hookLine: Arrian, Epictetus' student, boiled his teacher down into a little book meant to be kept at hand

lines: A BOOK THAT FITS IN A POCKET.
cards: Most books that change lives are too heavy to carry. This one fits in a coat pocket: around fifty short sections. You can read it on a bus ride and spend the rest of your life on it.
Nearly two thousand years ago, in a school on the western coast of Greece, a young man named Arrian sat writing down everything his teacher said.
The teacher was an old man with a lame leg who had grown up enslaved, and he never wrote a word himself. The student wrote it all, then boiled it down. Year two opens on the porch.
Today: the handbook for the road.

teach.b: Epictetus was born around the year fifty in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, and grew up enslaved. His owner, Epaphroditus, was a freedman who served at the court of Nero.
Somehow the young man was allowed to study with Musonius Rufus, the Stoic from year one who called plain food training.

Later he was freed and taught philosophy in Rome, until the emperor Domitian banished philosophers from the city near the end of the first century. Epictetus moved to Nicopolis in Greece and opened a school.
Arrian, later a Roman governor and the historian of Alexander the Great, took down his teacher's talks. Those notes became the Discourses; four books survive.
Then Arrian made something smaller: the best of it in short, plain sections.
Enchiridion is Greek: en, in, and cheir, the hand. Something kept in the hand. The same word could mean a hand-knife, a small blade you keep close.
Not a book for the shelf; a tool for the road. People have carried it ever since.
Marcus Aurelius thanks one of his teachers for lending him a copy of Epictetus' notes, and Christian monks later adapted the handbook for life in their communities.

teach.h: A YEAR ON THE PORCH, IN ORDER.
teach.b: This year the Stoics get read properly and in order: the handbook first, a section or two a day, then the Discourses, Seneca's letters, the whole of Marcus.
They're one school among many, read here on their own terms.

how: Many people who practice Stoicism keep a copy of Epictetus' Handbook nearby, or copy a single line onto a card, and reread it during the day.

o: a secret teaching shared only with close students
a long scholarly commentary on an older book
a small book of teaching made to be kept in the hand

p: the student who took the notes

s: he wrote nothing; his student Arrian wrote down his teaching and boiled it down.
he was enslaved as a young man and later freed, then taught in Rome and Nicopolis.

games.q: you're Arrian. your teacher's talks fill notebooks, and people want something they can carry. what do you make?
o: a little book of the best of it, kept in the hand.
nothing: tell them to come to class.
games.why: Arrian kept the long Discourses and also made the short Handbook, plain sections meant to be carried, not shelved.

practice: Write one line from year one that you want close, on a scrap of paper or in your phone's notes: maybe breathe, maybe look how far. Fold it small and tuck it in a pocket, a wallet or behind your phone case.
Rest your hand where the note is, feel how small and near it is, and breathe with the line under your hand.

wordCard.voice: Enchiridion. Greek for something kept in the hand: Epictetus' teaching, boiled down by his student Arrian, small enough to carry. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from en, in, and cheir, hand: something kept in the hand.

carryVoice: Your line: keep it at hand. A small book, and a small note, both made to travel. Day three hundred thirty-two, done.

sources.ref: Discourses, Arrian's letter to Lucius Gellius
